items.text: 1 · The Big Picture of a GPT

Start with the job of the whole file. A GPT reads a row of token ids, which are whole numbers that stand for pieces of text, and for each position it scores every word in its vocabulary as a guess for what comes next. This is called next-token prediction.

The file's first lines claim that the entire model lives in this one place. Read them as a map of what you are about to open.

You now have the model's job: token ids in, one score per vocabulary word out for each position. The docstring (lines 1-8) says all of it sits in this one file and points to the GPT-2 code from OpenAI and the Hugging Face version as references. Next, 1.2 looks at GPTConfig, the few numbers that decide how big every one of these pieces is.

The file builds from small parts to the whole. Each class only uses classes defined above it, so you can read top to bottom without jumping ahead.

Look at the order and the start lines. Block (line 94) is the first class that uses the others: its __init__ creates two LayerNorms, a CausalSelfAttention and an MLP (lines 98-101). GPT comes last, at line 118.

The three small pieces feed Block, and Block is stacked inside GPT. GPTConfig is the settings class that GPT takes in. Next, 1.2 looks at GPTConfig, the few numbers that decide how big every one of these pieces is.

A GPT takes token ids in and gives next-token scores out. The constructor is where every part of that machinery gets created. Look at lines 126 to 133. Five pieces go into one transformer dict, and one more, lm_head, sits beside it. Read each line and ask what it holds, not yet how it is used.

You now have the six pieces and the lines that build them: two embeddings, dropout, a stack of blocks, a final norm, and the output layer back to vocabulary size. Every size in those lines comes from config. Next, 1.2 looks at GPTConfig, the few numbers that decide how big each piece is.

Read forward top to bottom and you see the whole model as one path. Token ids of shape (b, t) go in, and a score for every vocabulary word comes out.

Before anything else, line 173 checks that t is no longer than block_size. The position table only has that many rows. The middle of the path keeps one shape, (b, t, n_embd), through every block.

The sum at line 179 adds a (t, n_embd) table to a (b, t, n_embd) one, so every sequence in the batch gets the same position vectors. Every block and ln_f keep the shape; only lm_head changes the last size, from n_embd to vocab_size. Next, 1.2 looks at GPTConfig, the few numbers that decide how big each of these pieces is.
forward ends in two branches. With targets, lm_head scores every position and a loss is computed. Without them, it scores only the last position, because only the next token is needed.

Training gives t rows of scores and generation gives 1. The list [-1] keeps the time dimension, so the output stays (b, 1, vocab_size). Next, 1.2 looks at GPTConfig, the numbers that set the size of pieces like lm_head.

Everything so far was the model: token ids in, next-token scores out. The rest of the file is not part of that path. Three methods on GPT help around it, and you can skip them while reading the model itself.

You can now name the three supporting tools: from_pretrained loads GPT-2 weights, configure_optimizers builds the optimizer, and estimate_mfu measures throughput. Later sections cover each one. Next, 1.2 looks at GPTConfig, the few numbers that decide how big every piece is.
Before moving on, here is what this section settled.

blocks.title: GPT as a Next‑Token Predictor
blocks.body:
A GPT reads a sequence of token IDs, one after another. For each position it computes a score for every word in its vocabulary, indicating how likely that word is to appear next.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Token IDs → Scores for each vocab word","caption":"Each row shows the probability scores the model assigns to every vocabulary token as the next word.","kind":"matrix","layout":"teaching","columns":["vocab A","vocab B","vocab C"],"rows":[{"id":"token-101","heading":"token 101","cells":["0.12","0.45","0.43"]},{"id":"token-102","heading":"token 102","cells":["0.30","0.25","0.45"]},{"id":"token-103","heading":"token 103","cells":["0.60","0.20","0.20"]}]}}
```

The scores are turned into probabilities and the highest‑scoring word is the model’s prediction. In other words, the model’s sole job is to predict the next token given all previous tokens.

The opening docstring confirms this: it promises a “Full definition of a GPT Language Model, all of it in this single file.”

questions.text: What determines the shape of the score matrix for a given input?
How does the model turn raw scores into a probability distribution?
Can the next‑token prediction be used for tasks beyond text generation?

blocks.promptUsed: /explain What does it mean that a GPT is a next-token predictor, given the file's opening docstring: "Full definition of a GPT Language Model, all of it in this single file."? Show it on a row of token ids going in, and for each position one score per vocabulary word coming out for what comes next. Do not cover how the model is sized or the order of its parts. Afterwards the reader should be able to state the model's job in one sentence and point at the docstring that says it is all in this file.

narration.script: Imagine a line of token IDs entering a machine, each ID waiting its turn. At the first slot the model looks at that single ID and instantly produces a score for every word it knows, asking which word could follow. At the second slot it has seen two IDs, and again it writes a score for each vocabulary entry, now reflecting what comes after those two. This repeats for every position, so the model never predicts a whole sentence at once; it only ever asks, given everything so far, what is the next token? The key is that the scores are computed for the entire vocabulary each time, not just for a single candidate. Think of a weather forecast that lists a probability for rain, sun, snow, and every other condition for each hour, rather than picking one and ignoring the rest. A common mistake is to imagine the model choosing a word first and then evaluating its likelihood. In reality the likelihoods are all calculated first, and the highest one is selected as the prediction. To see the model’s job in one sentence: it assigns a probability to every possible next token based on the tokens it has already read. The opening docstring reminds you that this whole definition lives in a single file, so you can point to it as the source of that description.

cells.source:
# Two branches of `forward`
This mimics lines 184-191 with numpy. `x` stands for the hidden states after `ln_f`, shape (b, t, n_embd). `W` stands for `lm_head`, a linear map from n_embd to vocab_size. Change `t` in the next cell and rerun everything.

import numpy as np
t = 5          # number of tokens: change me
b, n_embd, vocab = 1, 8, 10
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=(b, t, n_embd))      # hidden states
W = rng.normal(size=(n_embd, vocab))     # stands in for lm_head
targets = rng.integers(0, vocab, size=(b, t))
print(x.shape, W.shape, targets)

## Branch 1: targets given (lines 186-187)
Score every position, then cross-entropy. For each row, the loss is $-\log \mathrm{softmax}(\text{logits})_{\text{target}}$, averaged over rows.

logits_train = x @ W                      # (b, t, vocab)
flat = logits_train.reshape(-1, vocab)    # like logits.view(-1, size(-1))
flat_t = targets.reshape(-1)              # like targets.view(-1)
m = flat.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
logp = flat - m - np.log(np.exp(flat - m).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
loss = -logp[np.arange(len(flat_t)), flat_t].mean()
print('training logits shape:', logits_train.shape)
print('loss:', loss)

## Branch 2: no targets (line 190)
`x[:, [-1], :]` keeps only the last position. The list `[-1]` keeps the time axis, so the shape is (b, 1, vocab), not (b, vocab).

logits_gen = x[:, [-1], :] @ W
print('generation logits shape:', logits_gen.shape)
print('with plain -1:', (x[:, -1, :] @ W).shape)
print('last row matches training row:', np.allclose(logits_gen[0, 0], logits_train[0, -1]))

The last check is why the shortcut is safe: the final row is the same score either way, and generation skips the other t-1 rows.

**Try it:** set `t = 1`, then `t = 20`, and rerun. Training rows follow t, and generation stays at 1.

blocks.title: GPT __init__ components in order
blocks.body:
Line 127 creates `wte`, an embedding that maps each token index to a vector of size `n_embd`.

Line 128 builds `wpe`, another embedding that supplies a positional vector for each position up to `block_size`.

Line 129 adds `drop`, a dropout layer that randomly zeroes elements with probability `config.dropout` during training.

Line 130 constructs `h`, a `ModuleList` of `Block` modules, one for each of the `n_layer` transformer layers.

Line 131 defines `ln_f`, a layer‑norm that normalizes the final hidden state across the embedding dimension.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"kind":"layers","title":"GPT initialization layers","layers":[{"label":"Token embedding (wte)"},{"label":"Position embedding (wpe)"},{"label":"Dropout (drop)"},{"label":"Transformer blocks (h)"},{"label":"Final LayerNorm (ln_f)"},{"label":"LM head (lm_head)"}]}}
```

Line 133 creates `lm_head`, a linear projection that maps the final hidden vector back to vocabulary logits, without a bias term.

blocks.title: Supporting utilities in the GPT‑2 model
blocks.body:
The model class provides several helper methods that are not part of the forward pass.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Utility functions and their purpose","kind":"comparison","columns":[{"heading":"from_pretrained","items":["Loads a pretrained GPT‑2 of one of four sizes"]},{"heading":"configure_optimizers","items":["Creates AdamW optimizer with decay and no‑decay parameter groups"]},{"heading":"estimate_mfu","items":["Computes MFU by comparing actual FLOPs to the GPU’s peak"]}]}}
```

`from_pretrained` is a class method that instantiates a model using a checkpoint of one of the four official GPT‑2 sizes. `configure_optimizers` builds the training optimizer, returning an AdamW instance split into weight‑decay and no‑decay groups. `estimate_mfu` measures training efficiency by comparing the achieved FLOPs per iteration to the theoretical GPU peak, yielding the model‑flops‑utilization ratio.

blocks.promptUsed: /explain What are `from_pretrained`, `configure_optimizers` and `estimate_mfu` for, given that none is on the path from token ids to logits? One sentence each. Use the lines: `from_pretrained` accepts only four GPT-2 sizes; `configure_optimizers` returns AdamW with decay and no-decay groups; `estimate_mfu` compares achieved flops to a GPU peak. The reader already knows: the GPT layout, `forward`, `logits`. Do not cover: `GPTConfig`. Afterwards the reader can name these as supporting tools covered in later sections.

narration.script: Picture a workshop where you have three separate stations, each holding a different kind of tool that helps you build and evaluate a GPT-2 model without ever touching the core forward path that turns token ids into logits. At the first station sits from_pretrained, a class method that acts like a pre-packed kit. The second station holds configure_optimizers. Think of it as the mechanic that prepares the training wrench. This division ensures that the optimizer applies regularization only where it is beneficial. The third station contains estimate_mfu, which functions like a performance gauge on the assembly line. After each training iteration it measures the floating-point operations actually performed and compares that figure to the theoretical peak of the GPU, producing a model-flops-utilization ratio that tells you how efficiently the hardware is being used. A frequent misconception is to assume that these utilities are part of the forward computation that produces logits. In fact, they operate entirely outside that flow: from_pretrained creates the model instance, configure_optimizers sets up the training loop, and estimate_mfu monitors the loop’s efficiency. When you encounter them later, recognize them as supporting helpers that prepare the model, organise the optimizer, and evaluate training performance, rather than as components that generate output.
